title: The role of perceived employability and basic psychological needs in predicting academic outcomes: A semiparametric SEM Approach
content:
by Laura Maska, Patra Vlachopanou, Dimitrios Kalamaras

This study examines how university students’ perceived employability (PE) and basic psychological need (BPN) satisfaction influence academic motivation and academic outcomes, with gender and university type as moderators. Drawing on self-determination theory and employability frameworks, a moderated mediation model tested via partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) on a sample of 699 undergraduates is proposed. Results indicate that BPN satisfaction was unexpectedly negatively associated with academic motivation, a relationship moderated by gender. Perceived employability showed no significant direct or indirect benefits for academic outcomes, and a slight negative mediated effect suggested that higher confidence in employment prospects can reduce academic motivation. Academic motivation, in turn, did not directly predict academic performance measures in this sample. Crucially, a strong moderating effect of university type was found: The positive impact of motivation on academic success was far greater in private university settings than public ones, leading to a high explained variance in outcomes. These findings highlight the nuanced interplay of career perceptions, psychological needs, and context in shaping student success. Theoretical implications for self-determination theory and employability research and practical recommendations for supporting student motivation are offered in different institutional environments. Limitations (e.g., cross-sectional design and single-country context) and future research directions are also presented.
author: Laura Maska
